chapters.title: Introduction by Gurcharan Das
chapters.summary:
Gurcharan Das frames India's IT revolution as the nation's cheeriest economic story, a quiet transformation that succeeded where broad industrialization failed, and he immediately challenges the conventional fable that software simply grew at night while the government slept. He argues the book proves a more nuanced reality: a deliberate, if unheroic, collaboration between a unique trade body, NASSCOM, and a handful of reform-minded officials who quietly cleared red tape. The anecdote that anchors the introduction is the story of Prof. P.C. Mahalanobis at the Indian Statistical Institute in Kolkata, a physicist turned statistician who installed India's first computer, the HEC-2M, in 1955 to model the Second Five-Year Plan for Nehru.

Das praises Mahalanobis for pioneering computing yet warns that his Soviet-inspired planning placed the public sector at the commanding heights, closed the economy, and denied India the export boom that lifted East Asia. He then walks through a telling illustration: a table counting how often the word technology appears in successive Five-Year Plans, showing a slow rhetorical awakening. A vivid scene follows from IIT Kanpur in the 1960s, where an IBM 1620 arrived literally on a bullock cart, symbolizing both ambition and infrastructural fragility, while Homi Bhabha and TIFR engineers R. Narasimhan and P.V.S. Rao built an indigenous digital computer.

Das recounts Indira Gandhi's intensification of the License Raj, with customs duties at 140 percent and income tax at 97.5 percent, and the five-year delay of a 1973 report that would have let private firms build minicomputers. By limiting each firm to fifty machines a year, the policy made viability impossible, and IBM's forced divestiture and exit unwittingly opened space for HCL, which launched a microcomputer before Apple's PC. The villain of stasis becomes the hero of reform when Rajiv Gandhi, a pilot who intuitively grasped computers, brings in N. Seshagiri, the architect of the NIC and the 1982 Asian Games computerization, to liberalize hardware rules in 1984-86, doubling the installed base and halving prices. Das then retells N.

Vittal's favorite Birbal parable, promising NASSCOM's Dewang Mehta that if he cleared the path to offshore delivery, exports would quadruple in five years, from 164 million dollars in 1991 to one billion. Vittal kept his promise by creating Software Technology Parks of India, where even a garage could become an export unit via an earth station. Das describes the STPI diagram that shows a single satellite link turning a modest office into a global delivery node, and he notes the telecom bottleneck under VSNL, which Vittal outflanked by threatening a rival Satcomm.

He closes with Y2K, which Das calls a tailwind that let Indian firms prove quality inside Fortune 500 data centers at an estimated global fix cost of 300 to 600 billion dollars, and with Jack Welch's 1990s visit to a GE back office in Bengaluru, where Welch marvelled at Six Sigma mortgage processing and declared anyone who hadn't been to India an idiot. By 2019, 1,250 multinationals ran 1,750 capability centers, and Aadhaar had become the world's largest biometric identity platform with 1.2 billion users, a journey Das says proves middle-class values, engineering depth, and quiet statecraft together let the horse fly.
chapters.takeaway: India's software miracle was not luck or neglect but a quiet partnership between entrepreneurs, NASSCOM, and reformist officials who turned policy bottlenecks into global delivery.
takeaways: Collaboration between NASSCOM and officials like N. Vittal mattered as much as entrepreneurial grit.
Early planning failures under Mahalanobis show how industrial policy can both seed computing and stifle markets.
Icons like the bullock-cart IBM and the Birbal horse parable reveal how narrative and symbolism mobilized export ambition.
Y2K and GE's back-office bets illustrate how a reputational foothold can convert a one-time windfall into durable capability centers.

chapters.title: 1. Ab Initio: The Indian IT Industry Discovers a New Normal
chapters.summary:
The authors open on 30 January 2020, a deceptively ordinary day of vegetable-price headlines and Bengaluru traffic, until at 1:33 p.m. the Union Health Ministry announced India's first COVID-19 case, a medical student who had returned from Wuhan to Thrissur, Kerala. The chapter uses the pandemic as a live stress test for an industry that had spent six decades building resilience. Early quotes capture initial complacency: Capgemini India COO Antoine Imbert saying global impact looked limited while business continuity plans were reviewed, and NASSCOM vice-chair Pravin Rao warning only of indirect exposure through clients with Chinese manufacturing. NASSCOM even convened its Technology and Leadership Forum in mid-February, only to confront a nationwide twenty-one-day lockdown on 24 March after the Jaipur cluster. The core anecdote contrasts two leaders' playbooks.

At Infosys, the Business Continuity Management team under Pravin Rao reactivated a handbook shaped by earlier crises, shipping 35,000 laptops and desktops to homes within a week, scaling VPN bandwidth tenfold and backend concurrency fourfold, and standing up a 24-hour help desk; soon 93 percent of the global workforce was securely remote. At TCS, Rajesh Gopinathan chaired a Covid Emergency Response Apex committee and pivoted from a twenty-year-old centralized campus model to Secure Borderless Workspaces, leveraging prior investments in agile workspaces, digitized governance, and cloud collaboration, reaching 90 percent remote work by late March. Gopinathan is quoted as saying the crisis leapfrogged TCS into a new model.

The chapter includes an illustration of the NASSCOM-government coordination flowchart that shows the Department of Telecommunications relaxing Other Service Provider norms to allow SEZ equipment to move home, with MeitY and the commerce ministry streamlining customs. Debjani Ghosh, NASSCOM president, is cited crediting that responsiveness. Client voices ground the transition: Mars Incorporated's Sandeep Dadlani, former head of Infosys Americas, expected a 20 percent productivity drop yet witnessed one of his smoothest financial closes because teams automated processes proactively. The authors reproduce a chart of digital acceleration where N. Chandrasekaran declares Default is Digital, noting that schools, courts, and farm cooperatives went online-only and that clients pivoted toward cloud, workplace transformation, and automation. Infosys leaders Nandan Nilekani and Salil Parekh echo the shift.

The conceptual framework is business continuity as accumulated organizational learning, not ad hoc heroics, and the chapter closes by arguing that the pandemic validated the Global Delivery Model's resilience, turned a physical colocation assumption into a borderless capability, and foreshadowed hybrid work as the new normal for an industry that contributes eight percent of GDP. This insight matters because it reframes how leaders think about execution under uncertainty, showing that disciplined iteration, trusted networks, and respect for long-term capability building produce outcomes that short-term opportunism never can. Secure Borderless Workspaces illustrates how a twenty-year-old operating model can be leapfrogged under pressure when governance is already digitized.
Government relaxation of OSP and SEZ rules was decisive, proving policy agility can amplify private resilience.
Client testimony from Mars shows productivity can rise during disruption when automation is delegated to delivery teams.

chapters.title: 2. Emergence of IT in India and Capability-Building
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks when and where Indian IT actually began, and answers by auditing the intellectual infrastructure that made a software powerhouse thinkable long before exports existed. The authors open with a crisp 2021 snapshot: IT at eight percent of GDP, fifty-two percent of services exports, 4.5 million professionals, and over one thousand MNC subsidiaries, then rewind to the question of firsts. The method is distinctive: they mine the First, Second, and Third Five-Year Plans as cultural texts, counting occurrences of technology, technological, and technologist to show how planning rhetoric evolved. The First Plan from 1951 is illustrated with a word-frequency bar chart that is almost empty, reflecting Nehruvian focus on agrarian and heavy-industry basics.

The Second Plan, drafted with Mahalanobis and his HEC-2M, shows a sudden spike in modeling language, with input-output matrices displayed as a figure, yet the authors dissect how the same plan seeded the License Raj. The Third Plan's excerpt includes a photograph of the TIFRAC computer, built by the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research team, as evidence of indigenous capability. Anecdotes make the abstract concrete. At IIT Kanpur, the first computer science course in India is taught on the bullock-cart IBM 1620, and students batch jobs via punched cards while faculty recount keeping the machine alive through dusty summers and voltage swings. At ISI Kolkata, a figure of the HEC-2M console illustrates the room-sized machine that ran national allocation models. The entrepreneurs arrive early: F.C.

Kohli persuading the Tata group to back Tata Consultancy Services in 1968, starting with punched-card services for Tata Power's billing, and the Patni brothers incubating their venture inside TCS before spinning out. A table of early adopters shows state electricity boards, Life Insurance Corporation, and the Central Bank adopting payroll and inventory systems, each case study including a simple flow diagram of batch processing. The chapter's central concept is capability-building as a three-legged stool: statistical planning, engineering education, and early domestic computer manufacturing combined with services experimentation. An illustration of the educational pipeline maps the IIT and Regional Engineering College expansion to the later supply of a million engineers a year. The authors quote extensively from video histories hosted at itihaasa.com, where pioneers describe soldering memory cores by hand.

The takeaway is that the visible export boom of the 1990s rested on two quiet decades of teaching, tinkering, and trial deployments in government and public-sector firms, a slow accretion invisible in GDP charts but decisive when opportunity finally knocked. takeaways: Mining Five-Year Plans for technology vocabulary reveals how policy imagination lagged hardware reality.
The bullock-cart IBM and hand-soldered cores show capability was built through physical improvisation, not just policy.
Early TCS and Patni batch jobs for power and insurance firms created reusable systems expertise before any foreign client existed.
Education pipelines from IIT Kanpur onward explain how a million engineers a year became possible later.

chapters.title: 3. Emphasis on Self-Reliance and the Domestic Hardware Industry
chapters.summary:
The 1970s are framed as a decade of forced self-reliance after the 1971 war made New Delhi fear Western denial of advanced electronics for defense. The centerpiece anecdote is the Air Defence Ground Environment System, ADGES, for the Indian Air Force, the largest computer-led electronics project of the decade, built using ECIL's TDC series and TIFR's design know-how under the Department of Electronics. The chapter reproduces an architectural diagram of ADGES showing radar inputs, TDC-316 minicomputers, and display consoles linked in real time, and quotes engineers who debugged the system in un-air-conditioned shelters. The DoE's twin strategy is laid out in a policy matrix figure: selectively import mainframes against software export obligations while licensing minicomputers to private firms to save foreign exchange.

That licensing produced the first hardware entrepreneurship wave, profiled with photographs and factory snapshots of HCL's garage in Delhi, Wipro's transition from vegetable oil to computing under Azim Premji, and DCM Data Products. A crucial policy failure is dissected in detail: a 1973 report recommending private minicomputer manufacturing languished for five years, clearing only in 1978 when minicomputers were about to be eclipsed by personal computers, and even then each licensee was capped at fifty machines a year, a figure the authors show in a break-even chart makes survival mathematically impossible.

The forced dilution rule requiring foreign equity down to forty percent forced IBM to exit India in 1978, a photograph of IBM's empty Bombay office marking the moment, which paradoxically gave HCL room to launch its microcomputer ahead of Apple. Customs data illustrated as a tariff staircase shows duties rising to 150 percent for computers, while a vignette recounts Narayana Murthy's five trips to Delhi to license a Data General MV/8000, only to find the price had fallen by two thirds while his license aged, and then paying 150 percent duty after refusing a bribe, recovering the excess only after nine years of litigation. Montek Singh Ahluwalia's memoir Backstage is cited to corroborate the absurdity.

The concept introduced is the hardware trap: import substitution without scale or competition produces neither self-reliance nor innovation. A comparison table of ECIL, HCL, and Wipro volumes versus global peers shows India's output as rounding error. The chapter closes by noting that because hardware was a regulatory minefield, ambitious engineers drifted toward lightly regulated software services, a migration the next chapter will trace, illustrated by a flow arrow from factory floors to code shops. The fifty-machines cap illustrates how well-intentioned anti-monopoly rules can make an industry unviable.
IBM's 1978 exit, meant to protect sovereignty, unintentionally seeded domestic microcomputing entrepreneurship.
Murthy's Data General licensing odyssey exemplifies how transaction costs can dwarf technology costs.

chapters.title: 4. Growth of Software Services and Mission-Mode Government IT Projects
chapters.summary:
The early 1980s are presented as a pivot where entrepreneurship fragmented by design: each new software firm picked a distinct lane rather than cloning the same product. The chapter opens with a quadrant map showing Infosys in services, Mastek in tools, Wipro in hardware-software integration, and Patni and others in body-shopping, each logo placed to emphasize differentiation at birth. The narrative then shifts to mission-mode government projects that acted as demanding first customers. N. Seshagiri's National Informatics Centre is the protagonist, and the chapter reproduces the NICNET satellite diagram that linked district collectors to New Delhi via VSATs, a network photograph showing a dish on a collectorate roof that readers today would mistake for TV.

The 1982 Asian Games computerization is told as a pressure-cooker anecdote: Seshagiri's team networking scoreboards, ticketing, and broadcast with Rajiv Gandhi's patronage while bureaucrats laughed at toys. A second mission thread follows the Indian Railways reservation system under the Centre for Railway Information Systems, where a flowchart shows the leap from manual ledger charts to the online PRS database that could confirm a berth in seconds, with a quote from engineers who tested the system by booking tickets at midnight in Delhi. The Indian government's selective import policy is illustrated by a duty table: 150 percent for a standalone computer versus 35 percent if tied to a software export commitment, a differential that nudged firms toward services exports.

The import license story returns with a photographed application file thick with notings, symbolizing why even well-connected founders feared Delhi. Seshagiri's role is summarized as architect who connected state offices by satellite and set the stage for e-governance, while the chapter notes that TCS's Burroughs mainframe, whose value exceeded all other TCS assets, was justified only because CMC maintained it for railways. The conceptual lens is demand-led capability: without sophisticated domestic users, Indian firms learned to build for foreign clients by first building for the Indian state under extreme constraints. A concluding figure maps mission projects to later commercial capabilities, linking railway concurrency to global banking systems and NIC district databases to later state data centers.

The authors argue this apprenticeship, funded by government missions, explains why Indian services could later promise mission-critical reliability abroad. The duty differential between 150 and 35 percent was a de facto industrial policy that pushed firms from hardware into services.
Railway PRS illustrates how a visible, citizen-facing system builds engineering confidence and reusable transaction expertise.
Each startup choosing a different lane prevented early fratricide and diversified collective learning.

chapters.title: 5. The Rapid Growth of Indian IT Services
chapters.summary:
The 1990s unleash is narrated as the convergence of deregulation, diaspora, and a satellite fix. The spark is economics: the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis and Manmohan Singh's reforms that devalued the rupee and relaxed licensing, illustrated with a rupee-dollar chart that suddenly made Indian person-months globally cheap. The human spark is the N. Vittal-Dewang Mehta partnership. The chapter recounts the celebrated NASSCOM meeting where Vittal demanded a Birbal-like guarantee that exports would quadruple to one billion dollars in five years, and Mehta recklessly accepted, a moment captured in a reproduced meeting photograph where Mehta's grin contrasts with officials' skepticism. Revenue did not just quadruple; a log-scale growth curve shows revenues from under 200 million in 1991 to five billion by 2000, then fifty billion the next decade, then two hundred billion.

The technical enabler is the Software Technology Parks scheme gazette notification, reproduced as a facsimile, whose elegant fiction allowed a garage with an STPI earth station to be a bonded export zone. A schematic shows an STP hub aggregating 64 kbps links to clients in the US, bypassing VSNL's international gateway, which the chapter details as the bête noire that placed endless objections until Vittal threatened to create a competing Satcomm government company. Liberalization continues under Rajiv Gandhi's 1984 and 1986 computer policies, charted as a stepwise drop in prices and doubling of installations. Y2K becomes the demand shock: a world map shading Fortune 500 headquarters that sent code to India, with an inset cost estimate of 300 to 600 billion dollars globally.

Rather than just revenue, the authors stress reputational entry, quoting clients who first sent non-critical date field conversions and then opened core systems. Jack Welch's GE story returns, now with a floor plan of the Six Sigma mortgage processing center in Bengaluru, where Welch saw graduates queuing for back-office work he could not staff in the US. The chapter also maps body-shopping to offshore via a delivery-model evolution diagram from on-site to offsite to offshore to global delivery, with 24-hour follow-the-sun arrows. Competitive illustrations include a price-per-line-of-code comparison and a quality maturity curve showing CMM Level 5 certifications clustering in India. The concept is the flywheel of reputation plus delivery, where each successful project lowered perceived risk for the next, and STPI eliminated the last physical constraint.

Vittal's Birbal bargain illustrates how a public quantitative target can coordinate private investment.

Delivery-model evolution from body-shopping to Global Delivery explains how cost advantage became structural reliability.

chapters.title: 6. Indian IT Comes of Age
chapters.summary:
By the 2000s Indian IT ceases to be a cheap alternative and becomes an inventive extension of global R&D. The chapter opens with a 2019 census figure: 1,250 foreign firms operating 1,750 capability centers, a density map of Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune shaded by center count, and a headcount note that IBM India alone employs more than a lakh. Anecdotes shift from founders to intrapreneurs. At Cisco Bengaluru, a team builds the ASR 901 cell-site router, photographed in a lab where Indian engineers test synchronization under monsoon humidity, a product now deployed worldwide. At Veritas Pune, engineers develop a cluster server and a financial replication engine, their commit histories shown as a code-contribution chart where Pune dots dominate.

The talent spillover effect is illustrated with a founder-tree diagram: alumni of services majors who leave to create unicorns, with arrows from Infosys, Wipro, and Cognizant to Flipkart, Ola, and Freshworks. The chapter revisits engineering education with a bar chart of a million engineering graduates a year, paired with a photo of a placement hall, and notes that multinational R&D centers began as extensions of headquarters departments before becoming autonomous inventors who file patents locally. A quality narrative threads through: the CMM and later Agile maturity curves, and client testimony from Amex, Walmart, and Boeing describing Indians owning entire subsystems. The authors also chronicle governance maturation: Infosys's ESOP program and its when in doubt, disclose norm, shown via a disclosure frequency chart versus peers, and Wipro's internal audit practices.

A counterpoint table acknowledges persistent gaps in product platforms versus services depth. The concept is coming of age as the shift from labor arbitrage to knowledge arbitrage, where the Global Delivery Model is no longer just about time zones but about deep domain expertise in telecom, finance, and aerospace. The chapter includes a revealing figure of value migration from coding to consulting and product engineering, and closes with a quote from Satya Nadella about Indian innovations in hardware, services, and skills now serving the world's digital imperative, reinforcing that the center of gravity has moved, not just the cost base.

Cisco and Veritas vignettes demonstrate how R&D mandates migrate from support to ownership when trust accumulates.

chapters.title: 7. Quo Vadis: Where Are We Heading?
chapters.summary:
The final chapter turns from history to horizon, asking where the Indian IT story points after six decades that took it from the HEC-2M room to borderless workspaces. The authors organize the future into three overlapping arcs, illustrated as a Venn diagram of services, products, and platforms, with Digital India at the intersection. The first arc is the continuing evolution of services into cloud, AI, and cybersecurity, with a spending forecast chart showing cloud migration as the largest enterprise budget line and anecdotes from TCS, Infosys, and HCL winning hyperscaler partnerships.

The second arc is the startup and product nation, where the Digital India, Make in India, and Startup India initiatives are mapped to outcomes: the count of hundred-plus unicorns, a map of co-working hubs, and a financing funnel from angels to late-stage PE. The chapter reproduces the India Stack diagram, layering Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker, and the Open Network for Digital Commerce as rails that private builders can ride. The third arc is societal digitalization, told through Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile, JAM, which cut bank onboarding cost from Rs 1,500 to Rs 10 via e-KYC, illustrated with a cost-comparison waterfall and a photograph of a kirana merchant accepting UPI. A vignette of farmers' cooperatives taking online orders during COVID shows how the rails reach beyond software.

The authors include a cautionary illustration, a two-sided ledger of promise and risk: data privacy, reskilling at scale, and the danger of premature product triumphalism without deep IP. They quote N. Chandrasekaran on the pandemic accelerating five-year roadmaps into months and Nilekani on population-scale platforms, and they revisit the economic stakes: IT's eight percent of GDP and fifty-two percent of services exports must now help create jobs beyond its own 4.5 million. The conceptual question is whether India can convert services credibility into product leadership without losing the reliability that built its brand. A final figure shows scenarios from incremental services growth to platform dominance, each with policy prerequisites.

The chapter closes by returning to the authors' video archive as a museum meant for future builders, suggesting that the next chapter will be written by those who treat the past not as nostalgia but as a playbook for building in public, with openness and scale as the new moats.
